paper_title: Modeling spatial evolution of multi-drug resistance under drug environmental gradients (Freire, 2024, PLoS Computational Biology)
core_reasoning_1:
\textbf{Claim.} In the non-spatial exponential-growth model with mutant frequencies \(f_i(t)\), constant susceptibility traits \(\alpha_i,\beta_i\), and mutant growth rates \(g_i\), the mean traits satisfy
\[
\frac{d\bar{\alpha}}{dt}=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g),\qquad
\frac{d\bar{\beta}}{dt}=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g).
\]

\textbf{Premises.}
\begin{align*}
(P1)\quad & M\in\mathbb{N},\quad n_i(t)>0,\quad N(t):=\sum_{j=1}^{M} n_j(t),\quad f_i(t):=\frac{n_i(t)}{N(t)}.\\
(P2)\quad & \frac{dn_i}{dt}=g_i n_i,\quad g_i\in\mathbb{R},\quad \bar{g}(t):=\sum_{j=1}^{M} f_j(t)g_j.\\
(P3)\quad & \alpha_i,\beta_i\in\mathbb{R}\text{ are time-independent},\quad
\bar{\alpha}(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i(t),\quad
\bar{\beta}(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i(t).\\
(P4)\quad & \operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g):=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i(t)(g_i-\bar{g}(t)),\\
& \operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g):=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i(t)(g_i-\bar{g}(t)).
\end{align*}

\textbf{Derivation.}
\begin{align*}
\frac{dN}{dt}
&=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{dn_j}{dt} && \text{by }(P1)\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^{M}g_j n_j && \text{by }(P2)\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^{M}g_j f_j N && \text{by }(P1)\\
&=N\bar{g} && \text{by }(P2),\\[2mm]
\frac{df_i}{dt}
&=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{n_i}{N}\right) && \text{by }(P1)\\
&=\frac{N\frac{dn_i}{dt}-n_i\frac{dN}{dt}}{N^2} && \text{quotient rule}\\
&=\frac{Ng_i n_i-n_iN\bar{g}}{N^2} && \text{by }(P2)\text{ and the previous line}\\
&=f_i(g_i-\bar{g}) && \text{by }(P1),\\[2mm]
\frac{d\bar{\alpha}}{dt}
&=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i\right) && \text{by }(P3)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i\frac{df_i}{dt} && \alpha_i\text{ is constant by }(P3)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i(g_i-\bar{g}) && \text{by the replicator equation above}\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g) && \text{by }(P4),\\[2mm]
\frac{d\bar{\beta}}{dt}
&=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i\right) && \text{by }(P3)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i\frac{df_i}{dt} && \beta_i\text{ is constant by }(P3)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i(g_i-\bar{g}) && \text{by the replicator equation above}\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g) && \text{by }(P4).
\end{align*}

\textbf{Final Result.}
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\frac{d\bar{\alpha}}{dt}=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g),\qquad
\frac{d\bar{\beta}}{dt}=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g)}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
core_reasoning_2:
\textbf{Claim.} If spatial mutant frequencies satisfy the common-diffusion frequency equation
\[
\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial t}=f_i\bigl(g_i(z)-\bar{g}(z,t)\bigr)+D\frac{\partial^2 f_i}{\partial z^2},
\]
then the spatial mean susceptibility traits satisfy the Price equations with diffusion
\[
\frac{\partial\bar{\alpha}}{\partial t}=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g)+D\frac{\partial^2\bar{\alpha}}{\partial z^2},\qquad
\frac{\partial\bar{\beta}}{\partial t}=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g)+D\frac{\partial^2\bar{\beta}}{\partial z^2}.
\]

\textbf{Premises.}
\begin{align*}
(P1)\quad & M\in\mathbb{N},\quad z\in[0,L],\quad t\geq 0,
\quad f_i(z,t)\text{ is twice differentiable in }z\text{ and once in }t.\\
(P2)\quad & D>0,\quad \alpha_i,\beta_i\in\mathbb{R}\text{ are independent of }z\text{ and }t.\\
(P3)\quad & \bar{g}(z,t):=\sum_{j=1}^{M} f_j(z,t)g_j(z).\\
(P4)\quad & \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial t}=f_i\bigl(g_i(z)-\bar{g}(z,t)\bigr)+D\frac{\partial^2 f_i}{\partial z^2}.\\
(P5)\quad & \bar{\alpha}(z,t):=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i(z,t),\quad
\bar{\beta}(z,t):=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i(z,t).\\
(P6)\quad & \operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g):=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i(z,t)\bigl(g_i(z)-\bar{g}(z,t)\bigr),\\
& \operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g):=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i(z,t)\bigl(g_i(z)-\bar{g}(z,t)\bigr).
\end{align*}

\textbf{Derivation.}
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial\bar{\alpha}}{\partial t}
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i\right) && \text{by }(P5)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial t} && \text{finite sum and }(P2)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i(g_i-\bar{g})+D\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i\frac{\partial^2 f_i}{\partial z^2} && \text{by }(P4)\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g)+D\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_i f_i\right) && \text{by }(P6)\text{ and }(P2)\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g)+D\frac{\partial^2\bar{\alpha}}{\partial z^2} && \text{by }(P5),\\[2mm]
\frac{\partial\bar{\beta}}{\partial t}
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i\right) && \text{by }(P5)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial t} && \text{finite sum and }(P2)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i(g_i-\bar{g})+D\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i\frac{\partial^2 f_i}{\partial z^2} && \text{by }(P4)\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g)+D\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{M}\beta_i f_i\right) && \text{by }(P6)\text{ and }(P2)\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g)+D\frac{\partial^2\bar{\beta}}{\partial z^2} && \text{by }(P5).
\end{align*}

\textbf{Final Result.}
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\frac{\partial\bar{\alpha}}{\partial t}=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\alpha,g)+D\frac{\partial^2\bar{\alpha}}{\partial z^2},\qquad
\frac{\partial\bar{\beta}}{\partial t}=\operatorname{Cov}_{x}(\beta,g)+D\frac{\partial^2\bar{\beta}}{\partial z^2}}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
core_reasoning_4:
\textbf{Claim.} For
\[
\frac{\partial n}{\partial t}=g(z)n+D\frac{\partial^2 n}{\partial z^2},\qquad n(0,t)=n(L,t)=0,
\]
with \(g(z)=g_{\max}g_0(z)\) and \(\varepsilon:=g_{\max}L^2/D\ll 1\), the paper's first-order principal eigenvalue approximation is
\[
\lambda_1=-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g(z)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz+O\left(\frac{D}{L^2}\varepsilon^2\right).
\]

\textbf{Premises.}
\begin{align*}
(P1)\quad & L>0,
\quad D>0,
\quad z\in[0,L],
\quad g(z)=g_{\max}g_0(z),
\quad \varepsilon:=\frac{g_{\max}L^2}{D},
\quad 0<\varepsilon\ll 1.\\
(P2)\quad & n(z,t)=e^{\lambda t}u(s),
\quad s:=\frac{z}{L},
\quad u(0)=u(1)=0.\\
(P3)\quad & \mu:=\frac{L^2}{D}\lambda,
\quad q(s):=g_0(Ls).\\
(P4)\quad & u(s)=u_0(s)+\varepsilon u_1(s)+O(\varepsilon^2),
\quad \mu=\mu_0+\varepsilon\mu_1+O(\varepsilon^2).\\
(P5)\quad & u_0(s):=\sin(\pi s),
\quad u_0''(s)=-\pi^2u_0(s),
\quad \int_0^1u_0(s)^2\,ds=\frac{1}{2}.\\
(P6)\quad & \int_0^1 u_0(s)u_1''(s)\,ds=
\left[u_0u_1'-u_0'u_1\right]_{0}^{1}+\int_0^1 u_0''(s)u_1(s)\,ds.
\end{align*}

\textbf{Derivation.}
\begin{align*}
\lambda e^{\lambda t}u(s)
&=g(Ls)e^{\lambda t}u(s)+D e^{\lambda t}\frac{1}{L^2}u''(s) && \text{by }(P2)\text{ and the PDE}\\
\frac{L^2}{D}\lambda u(s)
&=\frac{L^2}{D}g(Ls)u(s)+u''(s) && \text{divide by }De^{\lambda t}/L^2\\
\mu u(s)
&=\varepsilon q(s)u(s)+u''(s) && \text{by }(P1)\text{ and }(P3)\\
 u''(s)+\varepsilon q(s)u(s)
&=\mu u(s) && \text{rearrangement}. 
\end{align*}
Substitute the expansions from \((P4)\) into the last equation and collect powers of \(\varepsilon\):
\begin{align*}
O(1):\quad u_0''&=\mu_0u_0,\\
O(\varepsilon):\quad u_1''+q u_0&=\mu_0u_1+\mu_1u_0.
\end{align*}
Using \((P5)\), the principal unperturbed mode gives
\begin{align*}
\mu_0&=-\pi^2. && \text{because }u_0''=-\pi^2u_0
\end{align*}
The first-order equation gives
\begin{align*}
u_1''-\mu_0u_1&=\mu_1u_0-q u_0 && \text{rearrange the }O(\varepsilon)\text{ equation},\\
\int_0^1u_0(u_1''-\mu_0u_1)\,ds
&=\mu_1\int_0^1u_0^2\,ds-\int_0^1q u_0^2\,ds && \text{multiply by }u_0\text{ and integrate}.
\end{align*}
The left side is zero:
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1u_0(u_1''-\mu_0u_1)\,ds
&=\left[u_0u_1'-u_0'u_1\right]_{0}^{1}+\int_0^1(u_0''-\mu_0u_0)u_1\,ds && \text{by }(P6)\\
&=0+\int_0^1(-\pi^2u_0+\pi^2u_0)u_1\,ds && \text{by }(P5)\text{ and }\mu_0=-\pi^2\\
&=0. && \text{algebra}
\end{align*}
Therefore
\begin{align*}
0&=\mu_1\int_0^1u_0^2\,ds-\int_0^1q u_0^2\,ds && \text{previous two displays}\\
\mu_1
&=\frac{\int_0^1q(s)u_0(s)^2\,ds}{\int_0^1u_0(s)^2\,ds} && \text{solve for }\mu_1\\
&=2\int_0^1g_0(Ls)\sin^2(\pi s)\,ds && \text{by }(P3)\text{ and }(P5),\\[2mm]
\lambda_1
&=\frac{D}{L^2}\left[-\pi^2+2\varepsilon\int_0^1g_0(Ls)\sin^2(\pi s)\,ds+O(\varepsilon^2)\right] && \text{by }(P3),(P4)\\
&=-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+2g_{\max}\int_0^1g_0(Ls)\sin^2(\pi s)\,ds+O\left(\frac{D}{L^2}\varepsilon^2\right) && \text{by }(P1)\\
&=-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+2\int_0^1g(Ls)\sin^2(\pi s)\,ds+O\left(\frac{D}{L^2}\varepsilon^2\right) && \text{by }(P1)\\
&=-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g(z)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz+O\left(\frac{D}{L^2}\varepsilon^2\right) && z:=Ls.
\end{align*}

\textbf{Final Result.}
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\lambda_1=-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g(z)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz+O\left(\frac{D}{L^2}\varepsilon^2\right)}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
core_reasoning_5:
\textbf{Claim.} For a mutant with constant growth rate \(r_i>0\), diffusion coefficient \(D_i>0\), and Dirichlet boundaries on \([0,L]\), the first-order principal eigenvalue is
\[
\lambda_1(i)=r_i-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2},
\]
so \(\lambda_1(i)>0\) is equivalent to \(L>\pi\sqrt{D_i/r_i}\). For two constant-growth mutants \(i,j\), mutant \(i\) has the larger eigenvalue exactly when
\[
r_i-r_j>\frac{\pi^2}{L^2}(D_i-D_j).
\]

\textbf{Premises.}
\begin{align*}
(P1)\quad & L>0,
\quad r_i>0,
\quad D_i>0.\\
(P2)\quad & g_i(z):=r_i\quad \text{for all }z\in[0,L].\\
(P3)\quad & \lambda_1(i):=-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_i(z)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz.\\
(P4)\quad & \int_0^L\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz=\frac{L}{2}.\\
(P5)\quad & L>0,\ r_i>0,\ D_i>0\quad \Longrightarrow\quad
r_i-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}>0\Longleftrightarrow L>\pi\sqrt{\frac{D_i}{r_i}}.
\end{align*}

\textbf{Derivation.}
\begin{align*}
\lambda_1(i)
&=-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_i(z)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P3)\\
&=-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L r_i\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P2)\\
&=-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}+\frac{2r_i}{L}\int_0^L\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz && \text{constant factor rule}\\
&=-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}+\frac{2r_i}{L}\cdot\frac{L}{2} && \text{by }(P4)\\
&=r_i-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}. && \text{algebra}
\end{align*}
The positivity condition follows as
\begin{align*}
\lambda_1(i)>0
&\Longleftrightarrow r_i-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}>0 && \text{by the derived formula}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow L>\pi\sqrt{\frac{D_i}{r_i}} && \text{by }(P5).
\end{align*}
For two mutants \(i,j\),
\begin{align*}
\lambda_1(i)>\lambda_1(j)
&\Longleftrightarrow r_i-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2}>r_j-\frac{\pi^2D_j}{L^2} && \text{by the derived formula}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow r_i-r_j>\frac{\pi^2}{L^2}(D_i-D_j). && \text{algebra}
\end{align*}

\textbf{Final Result.}
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\lambda_1(i)=r_i-\frac{\pi^2D_i}{L^2},\qquad
\lambda_1(i)>0\Longleftrightarrow L>\pi\sqrt{\frac{D_i}{r_i}},\qquad
\lambda_1(i)>\lambda_1(j)\Longleftrightarrow r_i-r_j>\frac{\pi^2}{L^2}(D_i-D_j)}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
core_reasoning_6:
\textbf{Claim.} Under the first-order principal-eigenvalue approximation with equal diffusion \(D\), the difference between two mutants' spatial fitness measures is
\[
\lambda_1(i)-\lambda_1(j)=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl(g_i(z)-g_j(z)\bigr)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz.
\]
Consequently, a growth advantage of one sign everywhere gives the same eigenvalue ordering, while an antisymmetric growth difference about \(L/2\) gives equal eigenvalues.

\textbf{Premises.}
\begin{align*}
(P1)\quad & L>0,
\quad D>0,
\quad g_i,g_j\text{ are integrable on }[0,L].\\
(P2)\quad & \lambda_1(i):=-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_i(z)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz.\\
(P3)\quad & \lambda_1(j):=-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_j(z)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz.\\
(P4)\quad & \Delta g(z):=g_i(z)-g_j(z),\quad w(z):=\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right).\\
(P5)\quad & w(z)\geq 0\text{ for all }z\in[0,L],\quad w(L-z)=w(z).\\
(P6)\quad & \Delta g(z)\geq 0\text{ for all }z\in[0,L]\text{ and }\Delta g>0\text{ on a set of positive length}
\Longrightarrow \int_0^L\Delta g(z)w(z)\,dz>0.
\end{align*}

\textbf{Derivation.}
\begin{align*}
\lambda_1(i)-\lambda_1(j)
&=\left[-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_i(z)w(z)\,dz\right]
 -\left[-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_j(z)w(z)\,dz\right] && \text{by }(P2),(P3),(P4)\\
&=\frac{2}{L}\left(\int_0^L g_i(z)w(z)\,dz-\int_0^L g_j(z)w(z)\,dz\right) && \text{cancel common diffusion term}\\
&=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl(g_i(z)-g_j(z)\bigr)w(z)\,dz && \text{linearity of the integral}\\
&=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\Delta g(z)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P4).
\end{align*}
For a one-sign growth advantage,
\begin{align*}
\Delta g(z)\geq0\text{ and }\Delta g>0\text{ on positive length}
&\Longrightarrow \int_0^L\Delta g(z)w(z)\,dz>0 && \text{by }(P6)\\
&\Longrightarrow \lambda_1(i)-\lambda_1(j)>0 && \text{by the derived formula}\\
&\Longrightarrow \lambda_1(i)>\lambda_1(j). && \text{definition of }>
\end{align*}
For antisymmetry about the midpoint, assume \(\Delta g(L-z)=-\Delta g(z)\). Then
\begin{align*}
I&:=\int_0^L\Delta g(z)w(z)\,dz && \text{define the weighted integral}\\
&=\int_0^L\Delta g(L-y)w(L-y)\,dy && z:=L-y\\
&=\int_0^L[-\Delta g(y)]w(y)\,dy && \text{antisymmetry and }(P5)\\
&=-I && \text{definition of }I,\\
2I&=0 && \text{add }I\text{ to both sides},\\
I&=0 && \text{divide by }2,\\
\lambda_1(i)-\lambda_1(j)&=0 && \text{by the derived formula},\\
\lambda_1(i)&=\lambda_1(j). && \text{algebra}
\end{align*}

\textbf{Final Result.}
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\lambda_1(i)-\lambda_1(j)=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl(g_i(z)-g_j(z)\bigr)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz;
\quad
\Delta g\geq0\Rightarrow \lambda_1(i)>\lambda_1(j),
\quad
\Delta g(L-z)=-\Delta g(z)\Rightarrow \lambda_1(i)=\lambda_1(j)}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
core_reasoning_7:
\textbf{Claim.} Let two mutants have equal diffusion and piecewise-constant growth on \([0,L]\), with mutant \(1\) having high growth on the central half \([L/4,3L/4]\) and mutant \(2\) having high growth outside that central half. If \(g_{\max}>g_{\min}\), then their unweighted spatial mean growth rates are equal, but the first-order principal-eigenvalue difference is
\[
\lambda_1(1)-\lambda_1(2)=\frac{2(g_{\max}-g_{\min})}{\pi}>0.
\]

\textbf{Premises.}
\begin{align*}
(P1)\quad & L>0,
\quad D>0,
\quad g_{\max}>g_{\min},
\quad \delta:=g_{\max}-g_{\min}>0.\\
(P2)\quad & C:=\left[\frac{L}{4},\frac{3L}{4}\right],
\quad B:=[0,L]\setminus C.\\
(P3)\quad & g_1(z):=\begin{cases}g_{\max},&z\in C,\\ g_{\min},&z\in B,\end{cases}
\quad
 g_2(z):=\begin{cases}g_{\min},&z\in C,\\ g_{\max},&z\in B.\end{cases}\\
(P4)\quad & |C|=\frac{L}{2},\quad |B|=\frac{L}{2}.\\
(P5)\quad & \bar{g}_k:=\frac{1}{L}\int_0^L g_k(z)\,dz\quad (k=1,2).\\
(P6)\quad & \lambda_1(1)-\lambda_1(2)=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl(g_1(z)-g_2(z)\bigr)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz.\\
(P7)\quad & \int_a^b\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz=
\left[\frac{z}{2}-\frac{L}{4\pi}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi z}{L}\right)\right]_{a}^{b}.
\end{align*}

\textbf{Derivation.}
\begin{align*}
\bar{g}_1
&=\frac{1}{L}\left(g_{\max}|C|+g_{\min}|B|\right) && \text{by }(P3),(P5)\\
&=\frac{1}{L}\left(g_{\max}\frac{L}{2}+g_{\min}\frac{L}{2}\right) && \text{by }(P4)\\
&=\frac{g_{\max}+g_{\min}}{2},\\[1mm]
\bar{g}_2
&=\frac{1}{L}\left(g_{\min}|C|+g_{\max}|B|\right) && \text{by }(P3),(P5)\\
&=\frac{1}{L}\left(g_{\min}\frac{L}{2}+g_{\max}\frac{L}{2}\right) && \text{by }(P4)\\
&=\frac{g_{\max}+g_{\min}}{2},\\
\bar{g}_1&=\bar{g}_2. && \text{compare the two expressions}
\end{align*}
The weighted central integral is
\begin{align*}
A&:=\int_{L/4}^{3L/4}\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz && \text{definition}\\
&=\left[\frac{z}{2}-\frac{L}{4\pi}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi z}{L}\right)\right]_{L/4}^{3L/4} && \text{by }(P7)\\
&=\left(\frac{3L}{8}-\frac{L}{4\pi}\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{L}{8}-\frac{L}{4\pi}\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\right) && \text{substitute limits}\\
&=\left(\frac{3L}{8}+\frac{L}{4\pi}\right)-\left(\frac{L}{8}-\frac{L}{4\pi}\right) && \sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=-1,\ \sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1\\
&=\frac{L}{4}+\frac{L}{2\pi}. && \text{algebra}
\end{align*}
Since \(\int_0^L\sin^2(\pi z/L)\,dz=L/2\), the outside weighted integral equals \(L/2-A\). Hence
\begin{align*}
\lambda_1(1)-\lambda_1(2)
&=\frac{2}{L}\left(\int_C\delta\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz+
\int_B(-\delta)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz\right) && \text{by }(P1),(P3),(P6)\\
&=\frac{2\delta}{L}\left(A-\left(\frac{L}{2}-A\right)\right) && \text{using }A\text{ and total integral }L/2\\
&=\frac{2\delta}{L}\left(2A-\frac{L}{2}\right) && \text{algebra}\\
&=\frac{2\delta}{L}\left(2\left(\frac{L}{4}+\frac{L}{2\pi}\right)-\frac{L}{2}\right) && \text{substitute }A\\
&=\frac{2\delta}{L}\cdot\frac{L}{\pi} && \text{algebra}\\
&=\frac{2(g_{\max}-g_{\min})}{\pi} && \text{by }(P1)\\
&>0. && \text{by }(P1)
\end{align*}

\textbf{Final Result.}
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\bar{g}_1=\bar{g}_2=\frac{g_{\max}+g_{\min}}{2},
\qquad
\lambda_1(1)-\lambda_1(2)=\frac{2(g_{\max}-g_{\min})}{\pi}>0}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
core_reasoning_10:
\textbf{Claim.} For the paper's simple two-drug growth landscapes and canonical mutants \((0,1)\), \((1,0)\), and \((1/2,1/2)\), equal total exposure to the two drugs implies that the unweighted spatial-average growth proxy ranks single resistance above intermediate double resistance under synergistic interaction, ties all three under independent action, and ranks intermediate double resistance above single resistance under antagonistic interaction.

\textbf{Premises.}
\begin{align*}
(P1)\quad & L>0,
\quad x(z)\geq0,
\quad y(z)\geq0,
\quad X:=\int_0^Lx(z)\,dz,
\quad Y:=\int_0^Ly(z)\,dz,
\quad X=Y.\\
(P2)\quad & P:=\int_0^Lx(z)y(z)\,dz>0,
\quad q>0.\\
(P3)\quad & G_S(a,b):=2-(a+b)-qab,
\quad G_I(a,b):=2-(a+b),
\quad G_A(a,b):=2-(a+b)+qab.\\
(P4)\quad & \text{A mutant with traits }(\alpha,\beta)\text{ has local growth }g_{\alpha,\beta}^{R}(z):=G_R(\alpha x(z),\beta y(z)),
\quad R\in\{S,I,A\}.\\
(P5)\quad & \bar{g}_{\alpha,\beta}^{R}:=\int_0^L g_{\alpha,\beta}^{R}(z)\,dz.
\end{align*}

\textbf{Derivation.}
For the two single-resistant mutants, the interaction term vanishes because one effective drug concentration is zero:
\begin{align*}
\bar{g}_{0,1}^{S}
&=\int_0^LG_S(0,y(z))\,dz && \text{by }(P4),(P5)\\
&=\int_0^L(2-y(z))\,dz && \text{by }(P3)\\
&=2L-Y && \text{definition of }Y\\
&=2L-X && \text{by }(P1),\\[1mm]
\bar{g}_{1,0}^{S}
&=\int_0^LG_S(x(z),0)\,dz && \text{by }(P4),(P5)\\
&=\int_0^L(2-x(z))\,dz && \text{by }(P3)\\
&=2L-X. && \text{definition of }X
\end{align*}
The same calculation holds for \(G_I\) and \(G_A\), since their \(qab\) term is also zero when \(a=0\) or \(b=0\):
\begin{align*}
\bar{g}_{0,1}^{R}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{R}=2L-X,
\qquad R\in\{S,I,A\}. && \text{by }(P1),(P3),(P4),(P5)
\end{align*}
For the intermediate double-resistant mutant under synergistic interaction,
\begin{align*}
\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{S}
&=\int_0^LG_S\left(\frac{x(z)}{2},\frac{y(z)}{2}\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P4),(P5)\\
&=\int_0^L\left(2-\frac{x(z)+y(z)}{2}-\frac{q}{4}x(z)y(z)\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P3)\\
&=2L-\frac{X+Y}{2}-\frac{q}{4}P && \text{by }(P1),(P2)\\
&=2L-X-\frac{q}{4}P && X=Y\text{ by }(P1)\\
&<2L-X && \text{by }q>0\text{ and }P>0\text{ from }(P2).
\end{align*}
For independent action,
\begin{align*}
\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{I}
&=\int_0^LG_I\left(\frac{x(z)}{2},\frac{y(z)}{2}\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P4),(P5)\\
&=\int_0^L\left(2-\frac{x(z)+y(z)}{2}\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P3)\\
&=2L-\frac{X+Y}{2} && \text{by }(P1)\\
&=2L-X. && X=Y
\end{align*}
For antagonistic interaction,
\begin{align*}
\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{A}
&=\int_0^LG_A\left(\frac{x(z)}{2},\frac{y(z)}{2}\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P4),(P5)\\
&=\int_0^L\left(2-\frac{x(z)+y(z)}{2}+\frac{q}{4}x(z)y(z)\right)\,dz && \text{by }(P3)\\
&=2L-\frac{X+Y}{2}+\frac{q}{4}P && \text{by }(P1),(P2)\\
&=2L-X+\frac{q}{4}P && X=Y\text{ by }(P1)\\
&>2L-X && \text{by }q>0\text{ and }P>0\text{ from }(P2).
\end{align*}
Combining with the single-resistant value \(2L-X\),
\begin{align*}
\text{synergistic:}\quad &\bar{g}_{0,1}^{S}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{S}>\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{S},\\
\text{independent:}\quad &\bar{g}_{0,1}^{I}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{I}=\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{I},\\
\text{antagonistic:}\quad &\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{A}>\bar{g}_{0,1}^{A}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{A}. 
\end{align*}

\textbf{Final Result.}
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\bar{g}_{0,1}^{S}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{S}>\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{S},
\qquad
\bar{g}_{0,1}^{I}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{I}=\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{I},
\qquad
\bar{g}_{1/2,1/2}^{A}>\bar{g}_{0,1}^{A}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{A}}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
core_reasoning_11:
\textbf{Claim.} For any equal-total two-drug spatial profiles, including the paper's periodic profiles after normalization, the two single-resistant mutants \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\) have equal unweighted spatial-average growth under the simple landscapes, but their first-order spatial fitness difference is
\[
\lambda_1(0,1)-\lambda_1(1,0)=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl(x(z)-y(z)\bigr)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz.
\]
Thus equal total drug exposure does not force equal \(\lambda_1\) fitness unless the weighted exposure difference also vanishes.

\textbf{Premises.}
\begin{align*}
(P1)\quad & L>0,\quad D>0,\quad x,y\text{ are nonnegative integrable functions on }[0,L].\\
(P2)\quad & X:=\int_0^Lx(z)\,dz,\quad Y:=\int_0^Ly(z)\,dz,\quad X=Y.\\
(P3)\quad & w(z):=\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right),\quad w(z)\geq0.\\
(P4)\quad & G_S(a,b):=2-(a+b)-qab,\quad G_I(a,b):=2-(a+b),\quad G_A(a,b):=2-(a+b)+qab,\quad q>0.\\
(P5)\quad & g_{\alpha,\beta}^{R}(z):=G_R(\alpha x(z),\beta y(z)),\quad R\in\{S,I,A\}.\\
(P6)\quad & \bar{g}_{\alpha,\beta}^{R}:=\int_0^L g_{\alpha,\beta}^{R}(z)\,dz.\\
(P7)\quad & \lambda_1(\alpha,\beta;R):=-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_{\alpha,\beta}^{R}(z)w(z)\,dz.\\
(P8)\quad & \text{A normalized periodic profile }x_T(z):=Qp_T(z)\left(\int_0^Lp_T(s)\,ds\right)^{-1}\text{ satisfies }\int_0^Lx_T(z)\,dz=Q,
\end{align*}
where \(p_T\) is nonnegative and integrable with \(\int_0^Lp_T(s)\,ds>0\).

\textbf{Derivation.}
First, the normalization used for equal total drug exposure gives a period-independent total amount:
\begin{align*}
\int_0^Lx_T(z)\,dz
&=\int_0^L Qp_T(z)\left(\int_0^Lp_T(s)\,ds\right)^{-1}\,dz && \text{by }(P8)\\
&=Q\left(\int_0^Lp_T(s)\,ds\right)^{-1}\int_0^Lp_T(z)\,dz && \text{constant factor rule}\\
&=Q. && \text{algebra}
\end{align*}
For either synergistic, independent, or antagonistic landscapes, the interaction term is zero for a single-resistant mutant because one effective drug concentration is zero:
\begin{align*}
g_{0,1}^{R}(z)
&=G_R(0,y(z)) && \text{by }(P5)\\
&=2-y(z), && \text{by }(P4)\\[1mm]
g_{1,0}^{R}(z)
&=G_R(x(z),0) && \text{by }(P5)\\
&=2-x(z). && \text{by }(P4)
\end{align*}
Therefore their unweighted spatial-average growth difference is
\begin{align*}
\bar{g}_{0,1}^{R}-\bar{g}_{1,0}^{R}
&=\int_0^L g_{0,1}^{R}(z)\,dz-\int_0^L g_{1,0}^{R}(z)\,dz && \text{by }(P6)\\
&=\int_0^L\bigl(g_{0,1}^{R}(z)-g_{1,0}^{R}(z)\bigr)\,dz && \text{linearity}\\
&=\int_0^L\bigl((2-y(z))-(2-x(z))\bigr)\,dz && \text{substitution}\\
&=\int_0^L\bigl(x(z)-y(z)\bigr)\,dz && \text{algebra}\\
&=X-Y && \text{by }(P2)\\
&=0. && \text{by }(P2)
\end{align*}
By contrast, the first-order principal-eigenvalue difference retains the spatial weighting induced by the Dirichlet boundaries:
\begin{align*}
\lambda_1(0,1;R)-\lambda_1(1,0;R)
&=\left[-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_{0,1}^{R}(z)w(z)\,dz\right]
 -\left[-\frac{\pi^2D}{L^2}+\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g_{1,0}^{R}(z)w(z)\,dz\right] && \text{by }(P7)\\
&=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl(g_{0,1}^{R}(z)-g_{1,0}^{R}(z)\bigr)w(z)\,dz && \text{linearity}\\
&=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl((2-y(z))-(2-x(z))\bigr)w(z)\,dz && \text{substitution}\\
&=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl(x(z)-y(z)\bigr)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz. && \text{by }(P3)
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
X=Y
&\Longrightarrow \bar{g}_{0,1}^{R}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{R} && \text{derived above}\\
&\not\Longrightarrow \lambda_1(0,1;R)=\lambda_1(1,0;R) && \text{unless }\int_0^L(x-y)w\,dz=0.
\end{align*}

\textbf{Final Result.}
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
X=Y\Longrightarrow \bar{g}_{0,1}^{R}=\bar{g}_{1,0}^{R},\qquad
\lambda_1(0,1;R)-\lambda_1(1,0;R)=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L\bigl(x(z)-y(z)\bigr)\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi z}{L}\right)\,dz}
\]
\hfill$\blacksquare$
